title: Too many cooks? Solving Lidl-Trek’s 2027 GC dilemma
content:
Cyclist
Too many cooks? Solving Lidl-Trek’s 2027 GC dilemma

Too many leaders. It’s a blessing and a curse. When it goes right, it can win you Grand Tours. When it goes wrong… well, maybe let 2010s Movistar be the case study for that one.

The signing of Felix Gall for Lidl-Trek is certainly a notable one given his performances in the Giro d’Italia and Vuelta a España this season, however like Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe when they signed Remco Evenepoel, they now find themselves with a GC hierarchy to sort out, with Gall joining Juan Ayuso, Mattias Skjelmose, Derek Gee-West and Jordan Jegat in 2027.

Gall joins the team on a three-year deal from Decathlon CMA CGM, and it’s hard not to see him atop the pyramid thanks to his performances this season: second to Jonas Vingegaard at the Giro and third at the Vuelta, surpassing any Lidl-Trek rider in these races by far. He also brings over a ready-made superdomestique in Gregor Mühlberger, who finished 15th at the Giro and sat within the top ten before he abandoned the Vuelta on Stage 13. They won’t need any time to gel.

Derek Gee-West has been Lidl-Trek’s best-performing rider in any of the Grand Tours this year. The Canadian raced to fifth at the Giro as a new signing and was able to achieve a similar standing to his fourth place in 2025. Mattias Skjelmose had the team’s most impressive performance, however, finishing sixth at the Tour, and was the highest-placed rider at the Vuelta, though back in an unremarkable 13th.

Then there is Ayuso. Penning a five-year deal after unceremoniously leaving UAE Team Emirates XRG last season, he is the longest-contracted rider on the team aside from Mads Pedersen and his transfer drew much excitement. However it’s been a mixed debut season for Lidl-Trek. He topped the standings at the Volta ao Algarve and podiumed at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes but he finished a disappointing Tour seventh overall behind Skjelmose.

Lidl-Trek have also signed Frenchman Jordan Jegat from TotalEnergies, fresh off two consecutive tenth places at the Tour. Jegat has a great knack of muscling his way into high Grand Tour placings without much team support, and though Lidl-Trek will likely want to use him as a mountain domestique, he’s a strong backup option to have.

That is also just taking three-week races into consideration. Giulio Ciccone has finally given up chasing Grand Tour GCs, instead focusing on stage wins, mountains classifications and Classics, and he secured the maglia azzurra the Giro d’Italia this year.

There’s a lot going on at Lidl-Trek. If their ambition is to thrive in the Grand Tours, it seems a wild choice to continue adding onto their pile of GC riders instead of developing the talent they have. Who will want to ride as a superdomestique aside from Mühlberger? How do you balance Ciccone’s jersey ambitions and Pedersen’s stage hunting prowess alongside a podium at the end of a three-week race?

Out of all of them, Gall is the man that has come closest to winning a Grand Tour with his second place at the Giro this year. While the signings of Ayuso and Gee-West seemed to bump Skjemose down a peg, the Dane was able to dig deep and finisher higher than Ayuso when the pair raced the Tour together. He said to Denmark’s TV2 after failing to make an impression on the Vuelta, ‘Nobody else on the team who is here right now has achieved a better result in the Tour. So no one can take that role away from me yet.’

That yet will change when Gall joins, as he finished fifth at the Tour in 2025.

To suggest a tentative schedule for Lidl-Trek in 2027: it makes sense to send stage hunters and those with jersey ambitions to the Tour given the Pogačar/Vingegaard battle going on there. So, Ciccone and Pedersen to the Tour, plus home favourite Jegat to stretch his legs. That leaves the Giro and Vuelta open for a genuine attempt at the title. Giro lover Gee-West should join Mühlberger in helping Gall strike while the iron is hot in Italy, especially with both Pogačar and Vingegaard having ticked that race off now, and then send Skjelmose and Ayuso to Spain in the hope that Pogačar doesn’t go straight back to finish what he started.

The recent signings can go one of two ways. Either light a further fire under those already vying for GC leadership, build one of the deepest rosters in cycling, or end up collapsing under the weight of expectations and internal friction.

Let’s just hope there’s no tridents or quadrents in the squad’s future.
